title: Economic coercion can replace military confrontation while retaliation compounds bilateral trade losses
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35077; monthly bilateral GDELT event indicator calibrated against human-curated ground truth and estimated gravity-trade panel
geography: Global bilateral country pairs, with the United States-China pair highlighted in the reported trade-at-risk comparison

observations.period: Monthly bilateral panel; recent-decade comparison reported in the April/May 2026 working-paper version

denominator.unit: bilateral country-pair months and bilateral trade flows; the abstract does not provide one common household, firm, or U.S.-only denominator

hostility_layers.value: kinetic fighting, military posture, sanctions-context hostility, and routine diplomacy

economic_coercion_shift.value: the trade-weighted share of hostility channelled through sanctions contexts nearly doubled over the past decade

trade_effect.value: kinetic conflict and trade-context hostility are economically large and statistically precise; routine diplomacy has no detected trade effect
trade_effect.unit: estimated bilateral-trade response in a gravity model

retaliation_channel.value: directed hostility identifies a retaliation channel that compounds trade losses over several months

trade_at_risk.unit: billions of dollars of bilateral trade relative to a pre-escalation baseline in the paper's comparison

us_china_share.unit: share of reported bilateral trade at risk

observations.method: Construct a monthly bilateral hostility indicator from GDELT events, calibrate it against human-curated ground truth, decompose hostility into four layers, and estimate its relationship with bilateral trade using a gravity model and a directed structure for retaliation.
observations.uncertainty: The source is a working paper and the hostility measure is an authored event-data construction. The trade estimates are model-based and do not identify the incidence on U.S. households, particular firms, workers, consumers, or third countries. The $334 billion figure is relative to a pre-escalation counterfactual baseline, not observed lost revenue or a forecast; source timing, specification, event coding, reverse causality, and counterfactual choice matter.
observations.subgroup: Country pairs and bilateral trade relationships; the abstract highlights the United States-China pair but does not provide a U.S.-household or firm-level distributional breakdown.
observations.counterinterpretation: Sanctions-context hostility may be selected precisely when trade or strategic tensions are already deteriorating, and observed trade reductions can reflect demand, supply, policy, or third-country substitution channels. Routine diplomacy's null aggregate trade result does not mean diplomacy has no political or security value. A trade loss does not by itself establish coercive success or failure.

related_sources.claim: The international-power model treats asymmetric import dependence as a source of coercive leverage and reports that worsening geopolitical relationships can induce trade adjustment; it is a separate mechanism from the observed-event and trade panel here.
The reserves-and-sanctions study supplies a separate financial-channel comparator for sanctions and trade-policy uncertainty, including effects on dollar reserve holdings.

boundary: This record adds a comparative measured geopolitical-to-trade pathway and a retaliation mechanism. It does not establish a U.S.-only effect, household or firm incidence, supply substitution, public legitimacy, alliance durability, or whether economic coercion achieved a political objective. It must not be merged with the separate CRS timeline of 2025 U.S. tariff responses or with model-based claims about reserve status.
